record.original_question: Color the unit interval by k measurable color classes. An m-partition is a partition of the interval into m disjoint subsets, each a finite union of intervals, such that every part captures exactly 1/m of the measure of each color. Let c(m, k) be the smallest number of cuts needed, in the worst case, to produce such an m-partition. Is c(m, k) = (m - 1)k for all m and k?

evidence.quote: REMARK: The conjecture has now been proved by Alon.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $k, m \ge 1$ be integers. Suppose the unit interval $[0,1]$ is partitioned into $k$ measurable subsets $C_1, \dots, C_k$ (the "color classes"), each of positive Lebesgue measure $|C_i|$. An $m$-partition of $[0,1]$ consists of $m$ pairwise disjoint subsets $A_1, \dots, A_m$ whose union is $[0,1]$, where each $A_j$ is a finite union of subintervals of $[0,1]$, and such that for every color $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$ and every part $j \in \{1,\dots,m\}$,
$$|A_j \cap C_i| = \frac{1}{m} |C_i|.$$
The number of cuts of such an $m$-partition is the number of interior endpoints of the constituent subintervals (equivalently, the minimum number of points in $(0,1)$ at which $[0,1]$ must be cut so that the resulting open intervals can be reassembled into the parts $A_1,\dots,A_m$).

Define $c(m,k)$ to be the smallest integer $N$ such that, for every choice of $k$ measurable color classes $C_1,\dots,C_k$ partitioning $[0,1]$, there exists an $m$-partition using at most $N$ cuts.

Prove or disprove: $c(m,k) = (m-1)k$ for all positive integers $m$ and $k$.
artifact.status_search_result: This is the continuous necklace-splitting problem. The upper bound $c(m,k)\le (m-1)k$ was established by Noga Alon (1987) using a Borsuk–Ulam type argument, matching the easy lower bound. The conjecture is therefore considered solved.

status_evidence.title: Splitting necklaces — N. Alon
status_evidence.snippet: It is shown that k(t-1) cuts always suffice to fairly split a necklace with k colors among t thieves.
status_evidence.claim: Alon proved the matching upper bound (m-1)k, resolving the conjecture.
